questions.q: What happens to a local variable's memory when the function that declared it returns?
options: It remains allocated until the program ends
It is destroyed automatically as the function's stack frame is popped
It moves to the heap automatically
Nothing happens unless delete is called
questions.explain: Local variables live on the stack, in a frame created when the function is entered. When the function returns, that frame is popped and everything in it is destroyed automatically.

questions.q: What is the key difference between stack and heap memory?
options: The heap is faster and automatically managed; the stack is slower and manual
The stack is fast and automatically scoped; the heap is manually managed and can outlive the function that allocated it
There is no functional difference between them
The stack can only hold integers
questions.explain: Stack allocations are automatic and strictly tied to scope. Heap allocations, made with new, persist until explicitly freed with delete, independent of the function that created them.

questions.q: In `double* make_price() { double price = 182.35; return &price; }`, what is the bug?
options: The function should return an int instead of a double*
price is a stack-local variable that is destroyed when the function returns, so the returned pointer dangles
You cannot take the address of a double in C++
There is no bug; this is correct and safe code
questions.explain: price lives on the stack and is destroyed the instant make_price returns. The returned pointer then refers to memory that no longer holds a valid Trade value — a classic dangling pointer.

questions.q: What happens if you allocate memory with `new` but never call the matching `delete`?
options: The compiler automatically frees it at program exit with no consequence
The memory leaks — it remains allocated and unreachable for as long as the program runs
The program fails to compile
The memory is automatically returned to the stack
questions.explain: Heap memory is the programmer's responsibility. Forgetting to delete it after it's no longer needed is a memory leak — the memory stays reserved and unusable until the process ends.

questions.q: When exactly is a stack-allocated object's destructor called?
options: Only when the program exits
At an unpredictable time chosen by the garbage collector
Deterministically, the instant execution leaves the object's enclosing scope
Only if the programmer calls delete on it
questions.explain: Stack object destruction is deterministic: it happens the moment execution leaves the enclosing block, whether by reaching the end of the block, a return, or an exception unwinding through it.
